name: Bilal Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a letting agency on the high street, five of us and about six hundred rented flats on the books. I book the viewings, chase the gas and electrical certificates, file the tenancy agreements and log the repair calls for the maintenance man. I'm still the junior and the deposit paperwork still catches me out. But I use AI every day, it drafts my emails to landlords and sorts the repair calls by how urgent they are.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up leaning on AI so much?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm not the sharpest with the legal side, so I started asking an AI to explain the tenancy rules in plain words. Then I thought, why not let it draft the boring letters too. I still live with my parents to save money, and most evenings I'm at the kitchen table trying new tools while my mum tells me to eat something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and people got carried away. At work I'd keep showing the others the shortcuts, because the agency runs better when we're quicker. I'd probably post that the market sorted out the hype, like it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good world for me. I'm the one in the office who knows the tools, and that keeps me useful while I'm still slow on deposits. My worry is more that letting is a tough trade, and the big online agents keep undercutting our fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask the boss for a small raise in the new year, since I'm handling more calls than when I started. I'd keep saving, I've got about four months put by, and I'd like a deposit for my own flat by thirty. On weekends I'd keep sorting out the paperwork for my uncle's plumbing business, which he pays me a bit for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite comfortable, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the online agents. How real is that threat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty real. Two landlords moved their flats to an online firm this year because it's half the fee. If that keeps up, the boss might cut hours, and the junior is the obvious one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does living with your parents mean for you, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I pay my mum a bit for food and the rest I save. It's not glamorous at twenty-seven, but my dad did the same before he married. Family looks after family, that's how we were raised.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool** and people got carried away.
I'd post that the **market** sorted out the hype, like it always does.
think: Knowing the tools keeps me **useful** while I'm still slow on deposits.
The real threat is **online agents** undercutting the agency's fees.
do: Ask the boss for a **small raise** in the new year.
Keep saving toward a **flat deposit** by thirty.
Keep doing my uncle's **plumbing paperwork** at weekends for pay.
S0.quote: Two landlords moved their flats to an online firm this year because it's half the fee.
fieldNote: He uses AI **daily** to cover his weak spot, the legal side.
His threat in a calm world is **online competitors**, not AI.
Living with his parents keeps costs low; **family support** is a value, not a shame.

steps.text: Ask the boss for a small raise in the new year
Save toward a flat deposit by age thirty
Do paid weekend paperwork for his uncle's plumbing business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a threat, if you're willing to learn. At work I'd push the boss to use AI for viewings and repair calls, so we can compete with the online firms. Online I'd say people should stop waiting for government and start learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, booking, checking, answering tenants, that's my whole job, so the job as it is now goes. But I think there's a gap. Small firms like my uncle's plumbing business can't set this stuff up themselves. If I'm good at it, I could do that for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a little side business setting up AI booking and invoicing for local tradesmen, starting with my uncle and his mates. I'd do it evenings and weekends while keeping the agency job. I'd put some of my savings, maybe a month's worth, into a decent laptop and some software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. It feels like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job as it is now goes. How soon at the agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two or three years. The boss is cautious, but if the online firms use it, he has to. I'd rather have my own thing going before that day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents think of you starting a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would love it, he always wanted to run his own shop. My mum would worry I'm giving up a steady job. I'd tell her I'm not giving it up yet.

fieldNote: He reads disruption as a **business opportunity**, in line with his free-market views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people who move fast will be fine. At the mosque I'd say we need to look after each other and help the young ones learn. I'd say the government shouldn't try to block it, because other countries won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me more than I'd admit. My agency job is gone by 2028, and if AI can do any thinking work, my little setup business is gone too, because firms will just ask the AI. I'd have about three years where hands-on trades still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on helping tradesmen while it still needs a person to set things up, and charge for it. I'd also ask my uncle about learning plumbing, because that's hands-on until about 2031. I'd keep living at home and keep my savings, because that's my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited and scared at the same time, which isn't a nice mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your setup business goes too. Why do it at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because for a year or two, people will need someone they trust to show them. Old plumbers won't sit with a chatbot. That's a short window, but it's real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after the robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe I'd own something, a van or a small firm, and let the robots work for me. That's the only way I can see to stay on top.

I'd say government shouldn't **block it**, because other countries won't.
think: My **agency job** and my setup business are both gone by 2028.

S2.quote: For a year or two, people will need someone they trust to show them. Old plumbers won't sit with a chatbot.
fieldNote: He spots a **short window** where trust still needs a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so get busy. I'd tell people at the agency to learn now, not later. I'd say the people who prepare will do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build my side business into something real, and maybe buy into my uncle's firm. By 2031 I'd want to own part of a business, not work for someone. That's how my family has always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the setup business for the first two years, keep the agency job, and save hard. Around 2029 I'd talk to my uncle about buying a share in his plumbing firm. I'd keep using AI every day, because that's how I learn fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into a plumbing firm, with robots coming in 2034. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when the robots come, someone has to own them. If the firm buys robots, the owners make money. I'd rather be an owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money for that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, my side business, maybe a loan from family. That's how my dad bought his first van. Family first, bank second.

fieldNote: His answer to automation is **ownership**, not retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and it's a great time to start something. I'd encourage people to learn and build. I'd be the optimist at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about it. Ten years is enough to build a proper business and own something before it lands. I'd be thirty-seven, with a firm and savings, and hopefully married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the agency job for a few years while the side business grows. By 2030, I'd want to buy into my uncle's firm or start my own. I'd look at marriage in the next few years, because my parents are asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of things. The business might fail, or the big firms might crush the small ones. But I'd have ten years to try and fail and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger cousins about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, learn a trade, and aim to own something. Working for someone else is fine, but owning is safer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job and my business both go, and I'd only have three years with trades. What would help is family backing me and a government that lets small businesses compete, not one that blocks everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to live at home at twenty-seven. People laugh, but it's why I can take risks. My savings are bigger because my mum feeds me.

headlineQuote: My savings are bigger because my mum feeds me.
portrait: Bilal is the **junior administrator** at a high-street letting agency and uses AI daily.
He's **traditional** and free-market, lives with his parents, and values **family support**.
He sees AI as a **business opportunity**, setting up tools for tradesmen.
In fast worlds his plan shifts to **owning** part of his uncle's plumbing firm.
He's **calm** with ten years and anxious with two.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job and his side business both go.
whatWouldHelp: **Family backing** and a government that lets **small businesses** compete.
